title: Call trackers tell you what happened. Then what?
summary: Call trackers show where messaging was missed. This guide for enablement leaders defines the feedback and practice loop that must follow, with Hyperbound Initiatives.
body_markdown:
An enablement team sets up a tracker for a new talk track. A month later, the report shows where the messaging appeared and which reps missed it.


The report provides useful visibility. It does not establish whether anyone reviewed the missed moments, gave reps feedback, or helped them prepare for the next conversation.


Those steps may depend on a manager finding time between deal reviews and customer meetings. Some flagged calls receive attention. Others remain in the queue.


For the enablement leader responsible for the rollout, the question extends beyond whether the tracker works. What happens after it identifies a gap, and who is responsible for making that happen?


Quick takeaways


- Assign a follow-up action and an owner to every tracker you use.
- Aim to deliver feedback within a day, tied to the specific call moment.
- Give reps focused practice before their next similar conversation.


## What sales call trackers do well


[Conversation intelligence tools](https://www.hyperbound.ai/blog/conversation-intelligence-tools-sales-coaching) make recorded calls easier to search and review. Depending on the tool and configuration, teams can identify competitor mentions, examine pricing conversations, and track whether new messaging appears.


For enablement, that evidence helps answer questions that completion reports cannot. Are reps introducing the new positioning? Which teams are using it? Where should managers listen more closely?


Trackers also help narrow the review. A manager can start with relevant conversations instead of searching through an entire[recording library](https://www.hyperbound.ai/blog/what-sales-managers-can-see-from-call-recordings) .


These capabilities provide a useful foundation. The next requirement is a defined response to what they reveal. A report showing missed behaviors needs to connect to a process for reviewing the evidence and helping the rep.


## Where the follow-up process breaks down


The gap between tracking and coaching usually involves three operational problems.


### Configuration requires ongoing attention


Depending on the tool, tracker setup may involve defining phrases, examples, conditions, and exceptions. Someone must establish what counts and review whether the results reflect the intended behavior.


[Gong's tracker documentation](https://help.gong.io/docs/about-trackers) describes two distinct types: keyword trackers that detect specific words or phrases, and AI trackers that assess concepts and intent. The latter requires writing explicit questions such as "Did the rep discuss pricing?" Each type requires deliberate configuration choices, and neither is self-maintaining.


Messaging changes create further work. A tracker built for an earlier pitch may need revision before it can assess a new one. Some tracker configurations are workspace-specific, requiring separate setup in each workspace. In Gong, the competitive insight view requires a tracker named "Competitors" exactly, with no variation, or the data does not surface in the[competitive landscape report](https://help.gong.io/docs/understanding-your-competitive-landscape) .


This makes prioritization important. Each tracker should support a current coaching or rollout decision, with an owner responsible for maintaining its definition.


### A flag does not explain the correction


A tracker flags a call where competitive positioning was missed. That identifies a conversation to review, but the rep still needs to understand the opportunity.


For example, the buyer questioned whether switching from a cheaper incumbent was worth the cost. The rep responded with a feature list without asking what was driving the evaluation. Useful feedback would identify that exchange and explain which question to ask before discussing product differences.


A team-level percentage can show where to investigate. Coaching needs the context of the individual conversation.


### Follow-up depends on available management time


Someone has to review the flag, locate the relevant exchange, decide what feedback is appropriate, and deliver it.


When that responsibility is unclear, follow-up becomes inconsistent. Even with an assigned manager, competing priorities can delay the response.[Research on sales call review practices](https://www.avoma.com/blog/sales-call-reviews) indicates that sales managers review less than 1% of all sales calls, not because of indifference but because no system exists to help them prioritize.


The planning question is therefore practical: can the team sustain the follow-up process at the volume of calls being tracked?


## What a complete coaching loop includes


A useful process connects call evidence to support, then checks subsequent conversations.


**Check a relevant call.** Define the situations in which the behavior should occur. A competitive positioning behavior should apply to relevant competitive conversations, rather than every recorded meeting.


**Identify the missed moment.** Locate the exchange where the behavior was expected. Review the context before deciding what the rep should have done differently.


**Deliver specific feedback and practice.** Explain the opportunity and give the rep a short exercise focused on that behavior. If several behaviors were missed, establish which one deserves attention first.


**Review subsequent relevant calls.** Continue checking whether the behavior appears consistently. Completing a practice session is useful information, but it does not establish whether the rep applies the behavior with buyers.


This process gives each flag a defined next step. It also gives enablement a way to assess what happens after feedback is delivered.


## Why timing matters


[Just-in-time sales coaching](https://www.hyperbound.ai/blog/live-call-coaching-coach-the-call-youre-on) connects support to a situation the rep recognizes and may encounter again soon.


Consider a rep who misses an opportunity to clarify why a buyer is evaluating a competitor. Feedback that points to the buyer's exact question gives the rep a concrete example to review. A short practice conversation can then focus on asking about the evaluation before moving into positioning.


A general competitive messaging course serves a broader purpose. It may explain the market, the product differences, and the approved claims. The immediate coaching need is narrower: how to respond when that situation occurs.


Set a realistic response target, such as feedback within one working day. Where possible, schedule practice before the next similar conversation. The aim is to make the connection between the observed gap and the next action clear.


Try this: audit your tracker follow-up


List the trackers or call metrics you currently review. Beside each one, record:


- Who reviews a missed behavior.
- What feedback the rep receives.
- When that feedback should arrive.
- What practice follows.
- How subsequent calls are checked.


Choose one tracker with a missing step. For one week, have a manager send the relevant call moment and a short coaching note within one working day. Add a brief practice exercise before the rep’s next similar conversation where possible.


Record the time required and any delays. This shows what the process needs before you extend it to more reps or rollouts.


## How Hyperbound Initiatives fits


Hyperbound is an AI sales coaching platform that helps sales teams practice and improve their conversations. Hyperbound Perform is the part of Hyperbound that scores and analyzes your team's real sales calls.


Hyperbound Initiatives, a system for autonomous behavior change included in Hyperbound Perform, connects missed behaviors on real calls to feedback and practice.


### It works alongside existing call-recording tools


Initiatives can run on calls recorded by Hyperbound or imported from other recorders, including Gong and Chorus. Feedback and practice are delivered in Hyperbound.


Teams can retain their recording tools while using Initiatives to act on the behaviors they want to see during a rollout.


### Admins describe the behaviors and test the criteria


Setup takes place in Kota, Hyperbound's AI assistant, where you set things up by describing what you want.


Admins can describe the behaviors or upload source material, such as a battle card. They choose which calls count, who is included, and the start and end dates.


A test run on past calls shows what would be checked and what reps would receive. Admins can refine the criteria before publishing. Nothing is sent to anyone until publication.


### Missed behaviors lead to focused support


When a rep misses a behavior on an eligible call, Initiatives delivers written feedback and a short roleplay. If several behaviors are missed, it focuses feedback and practice on the highest-priority one.


The practice is built for the rep's next similar conversation. If no similar upcoming conversation is found, it is built from the call they missed, using the real stakeholder, company, and scenario.


The initiative continues checking eligible calls for its duration. The dashboard shows consistency across recent calls, with access to the missed moments.


For the broader approach to measuring rollout adoption, read[Your team is 100% certified. Is anyone actually using the new messaging?](https://www.hyperbound.ai/blog/certified-but-not-using-the-new-messaging)


For Hyperbound customers


Choose one behavior you already track and a small pilot group. Use calls already recorded in Hyperbound or imported from tools such as Gong or Chorus.


Define when the behavior applies, test on past calls, and review the feedback and practice before publishing. Talk to your account manager about setting up the first initiative.


## What to do next


Review the trackers supporting your current rollouts. For each one, identify the action that follows a miss, the person responsible, and the expected timing.
